A palpitation is the strange, often unsettling feeling of becoming suddenly and intensely aware of your own heartbeat — noticing it flutter, pound, race, or feel irregular in a way that is not normal for you in that moment.

Here is the key idea: your heart beats around 100,000 times every day, and you almost never notice it. It works quietly in the background, like a ceiling fan you've stopped paying attention to. A palpitation is the moment that fan suddenly starts rattling loudly — you didn't ask to notice it, but now you can't ignore it.

A palpitation doesn't feel the same for everyone. People describe it as:

  • A flutter in the chest, like a bird briefly flapping its wings inside you.
  • A pounding sensation, as if your heart is hitting the inside of your chest too hard.
  • A racing heartbeat, where it feels like your heart is running even though your body isn't.
  • A skipped beat or a sudden "thud," as if the heart stumbled for a moment and then caught itself.
  • A sensation felt not just in the chest, but sometimes in the throat or neck too.

Palpitation is not the same as simply having a fast heartbeat. The word specifically refers to the awareness and sensation of it — you feel it happening in an noticeable, bothersome way.

A doctor's machine might show your heart is beating fast during exercise, but you won't call that a palpitation because it feels normal and expected. A palpitation is when the feeling catches you off guard or feels abnormal to you, regardless of whether your actual heart rate is extremely high or only slightly off.

You will almost always hear this word in its plural form: palpitations.

Saying "I have palpitations" or "I experienced heart palpitations" is far more natural and common than using the singular "a palpitation." Think of it the way you'd say "chills" rather than "a chill" when you're running a fever.

Palpitations can be triggered by a very wide range of things, which is why the word appears in both everyday conversation and medical settings.

Common everyday causes include:

  • Stress and anxiety — worry, panic, or nervousness can make your heart feel like it's racing or fluttering.
  • Strong emotions — even excitement, shock, or fear can trigger the feeling.
  • Caffeine — too much coffee, tea, or energy drinks.
  • Alcohol and nicotine — both affect heart rhythm.
  • Lack of sleep or exhaustion.
  • Dehydration.
  • Intense physical exercise — especially if you're unfit or push yourself suddenly.
  • Certain medications, including some cold medicines and asthma inhalers.

Medical causes (when palpitations are more serious) include:

  • Arrhythmia — an actual irregular heartbeat.
  • Thyroid problems — an overactive thyroid can speed up the heart.
  • Anemia — when the blood lacks enough healthy red blood cells, the heart compensates by working harder.
  • Heart disease, in more serious cases.

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word: most palpitations are harmless. They are very common, very brief, and resolve on their own without any treatment. The vast majority of people experience them at some point in their lives.

However, palpitations can sometimes be a sign of an underlying heart condition, especially if they:

  • Happen frequently or last a long time.
  • Come with dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain, or fainting.
  • Occur in someone with a known heart problem.

In those cases, a doctor should be consulted. But in everyday, healthy people, palpitations triggered by stress or caffeine are generally nothing to worry about.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples showing how naturally "palpitation" (or "palpitations") appears in real life:

  • "She got her blood test results and immediately felt palpitations from the anxiety."
  • "He cut out coffee entirely after his doctor said it was causing his palpitations."
  • "The actor stood in the wings before the show, heart palpitations making him feel faint."
  • "Palpitations are listed as a possible side effect of this medication."
  • "The cardiologist reassured him that the palpitations were benign and stress-related."

In literature or expressive writing, "palpitations" is sometimes used figuratively — beyond its medical meaning — to convey intense emotional excitement or nervousness.

For example: "Reading his love letter gave her palpitations." Here, the writer is not describing a medical symptom; they are using the word dramatically to suggest her heart was racing with emotion.
The Verb Form (Just So You Know)

The verb form is to palpitate, meaning to beat rapidly and irregularly, or to cause someone's heart to do so. You might encounter it as: "Her heart palpitated with fear." But the noun form — palpitations — is far more commonly used in everyday life and medical contexts.

A palpitation is the uncomfortable, noticeable sensation of your own heartbeat when it suddenly feels too fast, too hard, irregular, or fluttery — a feeling that is usually harmless but always hard to ignore.
